artworks.title: Molly Hatch: Agency
artworks.description: Agency is a site-specific exhibition by ceramic artist Molly Hatch that transforms Fuller Craft Museum’s Atrium Gallery into a monumental jewelry box. In this immersive installation, Hatch reappropriates traditional Victorian jewelry motifs as symbols of feminine strength and autonomy. Through oversized ceramic bows, snakes, swallows, arrows, and celestial forms, she reclaims imagery once associated with prescribed notions of patriarchal authority over women, recasting these symbols as powerful expressions of female strength and liberation. At a time when questions of identity and gender remain at the forefront of public discourse, Agency suggests that asserting autonomy through the hyper-feminine can itself become an act of defiance. By reinterpreting symbols once used to define and control women, Hatch invites visitors to reconsider the meanings embedded in everyday forms. What once signified possession or prescribed roles is reimagined as a visual language of resistance, resilience, and empowerment.
artworks.imageCredit: Fuller Craft Museum

artworks.title: The Vessel
artworks.description: The vessel is one of the most enduring forms in human history. Created to hold, preserve, and transport, it has supported daily life since the earliest days of civilization. From these practical beginnings, the archetype has continually evolved. Today, vessels carry not only physical contents, but also meaning, ingenuity, and stories.Drawn from Fuller Craft Museum’s permanent collection, The Vessel explores the structure as both object and idea. Organized around three themes—Surface and Storytelling, Sculptural R/evolution, and The Natural World—the exhibition highlights the many ways contemporary artists reinterpret this classic form. Some makers activate the vessel’s surface as a narrative space, layering imagery, pattern, text, and texture to convey personal and cultural histories. Others subvert utility, pushing traditional forms into sculptural territory through material experimentation and conceptual inquiry. Still other artists look outward, taking inspiration from animals, plants, and geological processes to echo the rhythms of the natural world.
artworks.imageCredit: Fuller Craft Museum

artworks.title: Fiber Forward: The Judith Stern Weisman Collection
artworks.description: Based in the D.C. Metro area, Judith Stern Weisman is a celebrated interior designer and passionate collector. Known for creating spaces where art, craft, and design weave seamlessly into daily life, she has guided others in building collections and discovering the joy of living with contemporary craft. For Weisman, collecting has never been about quantity; it has always been about discovering works that resonate—objects that tell stories and bring warmth, humanity, and character to the spaces they inhabit. Her collection reflects a profound appreciation for excellence in making, material innovation, and the lasting impact of thoughtful design. In recent years, Weisman has generously donated works from her collection to museums across the United States, ensuring that these objects are experienced by today’s audiences and preserved for generations to come. Her gift speaks not only to her enduring love of contemporary craft but also to her belief in its power to enrich lives and spark meaningful connections. This exhibition honors Weisman as both a designer and a collector—someone who has lived with art in the most personal way and now shares that vision with us all.
artworks.imageCredit: Fuller Craft Museum
artworks.galleryName: Community Gallery (education wing; the museum calls it the Education Gallery)

artworks.title: Stories on the Planet: Asagi Maeda
artworks.description: Fuller Craft Museum is proud to present Stories on the Planet: Asagi Maeda, a finely detailed exhibition featuring the wearable art of Japanese metalsmith Asagi Maeda. A gifted storyteller, Maeda creates miniature sculptural worlds designed to be worn on the body. Created from wood, plexiglass, resin, enamel, silver, gold, and precious stones—and often intricately engraved or enameled—the evocative artworks offer powerful reflections on everyday life. Swimmers, musicians, readers, and dancers express joy, tenderness, and sorrow, reminding viewers that even the smallest objects can hold entire worlds of feeling. Born in Tokyo in 1977, Maeda has been creating since childhood, inspired by her mother’s art classes and her family’s connection to pearl-making. She studied sculpture at Tokyo Zokei University and later jewelry at the Fashion Institute of Technology in New York, blending fine art and craft traditions in her practice. Now based in Tokyo, she continues to create and exhibit internationally, while teaching wax carving at Jyoshibi Art University.

artworks.title: Forest of Here: Jeila Gueramian
artworks.description: Forest of Here: Jeila Gueramian is a textile-focused installation that offers a fully immersive experience integrating kinetic, sound, and light elements. The site-specific exhibition is composed of a symphony of materials, including fiber works, found objects, and upcycled components. As visitors explore, they are encouraged to discover the intricate details and tactile elements that animate the space, creating an activated environment and blurring the line between the organic and the technological, the familiar and the fantastical. Forest of Here will prompt visitors to reflect on the interconnectedness of all things and the beauty found in the fusion of art, nature, and technology. Jeila Gueramian is a multidisciplinary artist best known for her whimsical installations that merge repurposed and handmade textiles with technology. Born in Los Angeles, CA, she earned her BFA from Otis Parsons School of Design in 1991. After graduating, Gueramian worked in art departments and costume design before turning to create custom props, plush sculptures, puppets, and fantastical costumes. In 2011, she shifted her focus to fine art through a six-month residency at The Wassaic Project. Since then, Gueramian has presented immersive installations at institutions including Sattsgalerie (Stuttgart, Germany); Crystal Bridges Museum of American Art (AR); Columbus Museum of Art (OH); Children’s Museum of the Arts (NYC); and Katonah Museum of Art (NY). She currently lives and works in Brooklyn, NY and Wassaic, NY.

artworks.title: MORE CLAY! The Power of Repetition
artworks.description: Curated by Rebecca Cross, MORE CLAY! The Power of Repetition features eight artists that transcend the structural limitations of clay to build powerful ceramic sculptures through accumulation, repetition, and innovative feats of construction. The multi-media exhibition demonstrates the power of assembling multiples as a compelling vehicle for the artists to express their chosen subject matter as they transform this humble, sustainable material into something monumental in form and content. Exhibiting artists include Zimra Beiner, Bean Finneran, David Hicks, Kahlil Robert Irving, Walter McConnell, J.J. McCracken, Kate Roberts, and Vanessa Ryerse. A printed catalogue has been developed in conjunction with MORE CLAY!, with an essay by Fuller Craft Museum Chief Curator Beth McLaughlin, and will be sold while the exhibition is on view.This exhibition is made possible by The Hamilton Company Charitable Foundation and the Caroline R. Graboys Fund. March 27: MORE CLAY! The Power of Repetition Special Preview Tour

artworks.title: Chieftain's Bowl
artworks.description: Mark Lindquist was taught woodworking by his father, Mel Lindquist, a renowned woodworker who pioneered techniques of woodturning by incorporating grinders and sanders. Lindquist continued his father’s experimental approach in his own works, challenging functionality and embracing experimentation by creating rough forms with chainsaws. His celebrated technique yields “flawed” pieces that appear ancient and organic despite their realization through the use of machinery. "Chieftain’s Bowl" is an early example of Lindquist’s experimentation with chainsaw as a tool in the woodturning process. Its gnarled surface is characteristic of Lindquist’s works. For example, notice the grooves incised into the surface and the raw edges around the rim of the bowl. The process of making this vessel reveals and highlights the natural flaws in the wood, emphasizing the inherent beauty of the wood and subverting its functionality as a vessel. (Wood; 25.5" × 17" × 17"; Museum Commission with Funds Provided by 1985 Massachusetts Council on the Arts and Humanities New Works Grant)

artworks.title: Earth Drawings X, "Tanami Traces" Series IV-05
artworks.description: Australian ceramicist Pippin Drysdale incorporates elements of landscape into her simple ceramic forms. Using a knife, the artist incises the surfaces of her works to create fine patterns that evoke the earth’s topography. Much of her work is rooted in the Australian landscape and can be read as a meditation on color, texture, and land. "Tanami Traces Series V" is part of a series inspired by Australia’s Tanami Desert. The shifting lines traced onto the vessel’s surface echo desert sand dunes as delicate orange striations ebb and flow across the pottery. Drysdale transforms the surface into a topography that one’s eyes can traverse. The elegant and simple interior of the vessel allows for an appreciation of the form and its rich color, a hue carefully formulated by the artist. (Ceramic; 11.5" × 13.375" × 13.375"; Museum Purchase)

artworks.title: Brockton Tea
artworks.description: Steven Hansen’s ceramic works are steeped in his upbringing in the rural Midwest. Using the trompe l’oeil technique, he “tricks the eye,” replicating the grit and rust of Americana-esque industrial signage. His pieces are imaginative—the older works feature hand-painted images, logos, and seemingly metal parts. His innovative process uses a layering technique of underglazes, slips, and oxides to emulate the weathered appearance of metal vestiges of middle America. "Brockton Tea" is steeped in Brockton’s own history. One side of the pot is emblazoned with the words “Our Champ ‘Rocky’ Brockton,” and the image of the boxer Rocco “Rocky” Marciano (1923-1969). Born and raised in Brockton, Marciano remains the only heavyweight champion to retire undefeated. The other side features a lightbulb meant to invoke Brockton’s history as the first place in the world to have a three-wire underground electrical system, activated by Thomas Edison on October 1st, 1883. (Ceramic; 14.25" × 15" × 8.5"; Museum Commission)
artworks.imageCredit: Fuller Craft Museum, photo by Dean Powell

artworks.title: Stranglehold
artworks.description: Jason Walker received his BFA from Utah State University and his MFA from Penn State University. Over the course of his career he has participated in residencies, taught, and exhibited nationally and internationally. Walker’s ceramic works examine the impact that technology has on nature as well as on humanity’s relationship with it. In "Stranglehold" a snake wraps around the torso of a bird which makes up the body of a teapot. The surface, populated with renderings of birds and foliage, sits atop a ceramic base painted to emulate wood grain, while the snake’s body serves as the teapot’s handle and is eerily reminiscent of an electrical cord. There is an undercurrent of danger and anxiety as the snake appears ready to strike the bird. Like much of Walker’s work, "Stranglehold" grapples with contemporary society’s dependence on technology and the “stranglehold” that it has over humans at present. Walker states that his practice examines the way that “technology has significantly changed and continues to mold our perception of nature… Collectively, we see technology as only friend. Yet, technology is both friend and foe.” (Ceramic; 9.75" × 8" × 14"; Gift of Arthur S. Goldberg)
artworks.imageCredit: Fuller Craft Museum, photo by Dean Powell

artworks.title: Vortex Vessel
artworks.description: Jennifer McCurdy’s wheel-thrown ceramic works push the limits of structural integrity and echo the rotations that formed them. Her intricate forms translate natural patterns into powerful ceramic pieces made of translucent, unglazed white porcelain. McCurdy carves away sections of clay from thrown pieces to evoke movement, after which she carves patterns into the surface for increased depth and dynamism. McCurdy’s "Vortex Vessel" swirls upwards with power, evoking elemental natural forces. The curved body of the vessel strengthens the form and stabilizes it following the drastic alterations made to the original thrown object. McCurdy’s carving adds significant negative space to the work as well as surface texture. Notice the way in which light and shadow play across the whorled edges, an effect which is heightened by the contrast of shadow on the starkly white ceramic surface. (Ceramic; 13" × 11" × 7"; Gift of Dr. and Mrs. Arthur F. Furman)

artworks.title: Splash
artworks.medium: Found maple and leather conveyor belt, salvaged pine, and various found woods
artworks.description: Stephen Whittlesey is a Cape Cod artist who finds materials for his furniture in unlikely places. The West Barnstable dump and abandoned ship wrecks along the beach are where the artist scavenges for forgotten and seemingly useless items to create unique and often playful works of art. The inspiration for the "Splash" cabinet came from a rescued coiled conveyor belt found in the rubble of a condemned wool processing mill in Massachusetts. This curved form suggests the outline of an octpus. Illustrated by the undulating shape of the top and sides of the cabinet. It is easy to envision the warped old maple conveyor belt as seats for a television in the large central section, or “head”, of the octopus. The cabinet doors are crafted from worn and battered wood. Other materials for "Splash" include old, salvaged pine from a whaling industry supply house later converted to a marine biological laboratory. Whittlesey has successfully taken his penchant for the art of repurposing to demonstrate Splash’s connection to the lively marine world and the potential of what lies waiting at the beach. (Studio Furniture; 56" × 74" × 30"; Gift of Gail M. and Robert A. Brown)
artworks.imageCredit: Fuller Craft Museum, photo by Alex Hochstrasser

artworks.title: Riamato
artworks.medium: Fused and thermo-formed colored glass filet-de-verre threads
artworks.description: Toots Zynsky is an American glass artist best known for her signature filet-de-verre technique of glass blowing. Zynsky received her BFA from the Rhode Island School of Design (RISD) before moving to Seattle in 1971. There she co-founded the Pilchuk Glass School with other glass artists such as her former RISD instructor Dale Chihuly. Zynsky developed the filet-de-verre technique in the 1980s, pulling glass into hair-thin threads, layering them, and then fusing them into a single sheet that is formed into a vessel. Each thin thread of multicolored glass remains distinct, giving Zynsky’s whimsical curvy vessels a shimmering depth. "Riamato" is the Italian word meaning to be loved in return. The vessel is similarly poetic, with its undulating form and luminescent striations of color evoking the beauty of flower petals. (Glass; 9.75" × 17.75" × 10"; Gift of Chris Rifkin and the Artist, Gift by Exchange)
artworks.imageCredit: Fuller Craft Museum, photo by Dean Powell

artworks.title: Big Maple Leaf Bowl
artworks.medium: Maple leaves, Kozo paper, and Krylon
artworks.description: Kay Sekimachi is an American artist celebrated for her three-dimensional monofilament woven pieces as well as her baskets and bowls. Sekimachi’s work as a fiber artist was greatly influenced by her tutelage under Trude Guermonprez at the California College of the Arts. Guermonprez’s influence ultimately led Sekimachi to move beyond functional weaving towards a more innovative, experimental practice. Sekimachi was a part of the New Basketry movement in the 1970s and has taught at various institutions over the course of her artistic career. "Big Maple Leaf Bowl" is an ethereal vessel constructed of preserved maple leaves, which have been layered with paste onto a paper bowl base constructed by the artist with kozo paper. The decomposed leaves are translucent in places, with delicate veins crisscrossing across the structure of the bowl. This vessel is seemingly fragile, although the paste applied to the leaves renders the form quite sturdy. (Fiber; 7" × 7.5" × 5.5"; Gift of Pat and Dick Warner)

artworks.title: Split Birch Log Teapot
artworks.description: Eric Serritella is a ceramicist who hand-builds and hand-carves trompe l’oeil works inspired by the organic forms of trees. His work has been celebrated internationally and is considered both technically impressive and environmentally resonant. Serritella states that his practice is built around the way that “ceramic mirrors the environment’s fragility and durability—easily damaged if disrespected and yet invincible in its inherent beauty and longevity.” "Split Birch Log Teapot" is a functional vessel, with small branches extending out from the base form to create a handle and a spout. One side of the piece features the distinctive white bark of a birch tree and a large knot at the top, while the other has a deeper brown bark with a knot at its base. The carefully rendered surface evokes the irregular, organic growth of a tree, with splintered edges and bark that appear to have withstood the tests of time. (Ceramic; 17" × 17" × 6"; Gift of Frances and Leonard Burka)
artworks.imageCredit: Fuller Craft Museum, photo by Dean Powell

artworks.title: Horse Netsuke Pot
artworks.medium: Blown and hand-sculpted glass, horsehair, and leather
artworks.description: Based in the Pacific Northwest, artist Shelley Muzylowski Allen explores the symbolic resonance of animal forms through her glass works. Her use of black glass imbues her works with a reverent quality, encouraging appreciation of the forms’ curves. "Horse Netsuke Pot" is one of a series that Allen developed incorporating horses. The figure of a horse atop the vessel was inspired by Japanese netsuke figures. Netsuke are a traditional Japanese carved toggle, often carved in zoomorphic forms, which originated in the seventeenth-century as a means of fastening a small purse called an inrō at an individual’s waist. The artist’s incorporation of horsehair for the tail connects it with the bodily reality of the creature it represents. (Glass; 37" × 15" × 13"; Gift of the John A. Goodman Estate)
artworks.imageCredit: Fuller Craft Museum, photo by Dean Powell

artworks.title: Moon Jar with Octopi
artworks.description: Steven Young Lee is one of the leading contemporary ceramicists working in the United States today. Lee earned his BFA and MFA in Ceramics from Alfred University. In the early 2000s Lee spent two months in Seoul, Korea, learning about the history of and process of making traditional ceramics while participating in a cultural and educational exchange program based in China. His practice centers around deconstructing classical concepts of the vessel as a means of exploring his personal identity as a second generation Korean-American. Young Lee explores the tension between imperfections and beauty in his pieces which seek to walk the line between damage as a devaluation of an object or a marker of uniqueness. "Moon Jar with Octopi" is an excellent example of Steven Young Lee’s exploration of imperfection and breakage in ceramic processes. Moon jars are a traditional Korean pottery form created during the Joseon Dynasty that has become a powerful Korean national symbol. Traditionally, moon jars are milky white and 12 – 18 inches in height. The forms are typically made by throwing two hemispheres separately and joining them at the center, leaving a subtle seam and slight asymmetry. No two jars are the same, and the small flaws they take on in the creative process are seen as part of their beauty. (Ceramic; 13" × 13.5" × 12"; Gift of the John A. Goodman Estate)
artworks.imageCredit: Fuller Craft Museum, photo by Dean Powell

artworks.title: Red and Green Amulet Basket
artworks.description: American-Canadian artist Laura Donefer is known for her playful and extravagant glass designs. She often explores the apotropaic function of glass vessels, seeking to create pieces that produce positive energies that will protect their owners from misfortune. Much of Donefer’s artistic practice has centered around teaching; she has taught at both her alma mater Sheridan College and Éspace Verre in Montreal. "Red and Green Small Witches Cup" is from Donefer’s 'Amulet Basket' Series. Evoking a witch’s cauldron, the vessel bubbles over with turquoise and red beads. Each of Donefer’s 'Amulet Baskets' holds an amulet created by the artist as a “a container for love and hope.” Donefer sees the creation of these pieces as an act of healing, a means of expressing a hope for unity and peace in the world. (Glass; 5" × 6.5" × 3.5"; Gift of Marsha R. Gold)

artworks.title: Melting Pot II
artworks.description: A self-described “ghetto potter,” Roberto Lugo is a renowned ceramic artist whose work confronts the intertwined complexities of systemic racism, representation, and history. In his work, Lugo’s blends his incredible technical skill at hand-throwing pottery with graffiti-style painting techniques, creating pieces that confront classical forms of pottery and its associated painting techniques. He incorporates portraits of prominent Black cultural figures into his works as well, often those connected to his Philadelphia upbringing and his heritage as a Puerto Rican American. Lugo’s work disrupts the aesthetic legacies of heirloom porcelain potteries by inserting complexities related to the American experience into these traditional forms. "Melting Pot II" is one of a series of urns in which Lugo incorporates historic porcelain motifs with figures important to the artist’s cultural heritage as a Puerto Rican American. The base of the work echoes Greek pottery with its orange and black color scheme decorated by classical motifs such as the Greek key. This classical base has been graffitied over, a connection to Lugo’s past work as a graffiti artist, and the orange and black are meant to evoke prison uniforms as well. The body of the pot features a blue and white color scheme traditionally associated with Chinese pottery, with the figure of Puerto Rican poet and advocate for national independence Julia DeBurgos on one side and the rapper Ice Cube on the other. The artist states: “The choice of figures references the dissonance of influences in my childhood.” The lid of the pot is made of castings of Lugo’s hands in his position when throwing pottery. They sit on the top of the piece, recalling the process of its making but also potentially serving as a protective force, and an assertion of the deeply personal aspect that the piece holds in relation to Lugo’s own history. Lugo’s charged use of the porcelain clay body creates a highly personal interpretation of the classical vessel form. (Ceramic; 23" × 11" × 11"; Museum Purchase with Funds Provided by the John A. Goodman Estate Fund and Anonymous Donors)
artworks.imageCredit: Fuller Craft Museum, photo by Will Howcroft

artworks.title: Plait #00205042021
artworks.description: Bahamian artist Anina Major creates sculptural woven forms as a highly personal practice centered around her cultural identity. Her work addresses the tourist economy that controls craft production in the Bahamas and the alienation experienced by Bahamians who perform culture for visitors. Major’s practice is thus restorative, as she creates ceramic sculptures that incorporate techniques used by her grandmother, who wove baskets for sale within this exploitative economy. By grounding her pieces in her familial and cultural history, Major seeks to create pieces which will not deteriorate the way that vessels made of palms do, thereby preserving this practice. The works in Major’s 'Plait' series were inspired by the gradual deterioration of her grandmother’s handwoven baskets. Major seeks to preserve these practices by realizing them in the sturdy medium of clay. "Plait No. 00205042021" exemplifies Major’s inventive combination of patterns in clay and serves as a commemorative vessel, preserving the memory of her grandmother’s practice. (Ceramic; 16" × 14" × 9"; Museum Purchase with Partial Support from LaiSun Keane Gallery)
artworks.imageCredit: Fuller Craft Museum, photo by Will Howcroft

artworks.title: Baroque Boat Basket No. 5
artworks.medium: Copper strips, welded wire grid, copper slats, and wire
artworks.description: Growing up in southern New Mexico John Garrett’s parents raised him with an appreciation for Native American arts and crafts. Garrett studied weaving under Marion Stewart and Neda Al-Hilali at Scripps College in 1970. His practice incorporates alternative materials, with baskets made from plastic beads, repurposed tires, metal, and other matter. For this work, Garrett created an experimental basket form made up of fine strips of copper woven to create a metallic textile-like form. As Garrett has said, “These ‘boat’ forms imply not only containment but movement, travel, and change.” The piece itself is dynamic, with strips of woven metal overlapping and extending outwards, giving the basket a fluid outer appearance. (Basket; 17.5" x 28" x 10"; Gift of Sandy and Norman Mitchell)
artworks.imageCredit: Fuller Craft Museum, photo by Will Howcroft

artworks.title: Large Stack Pot
artworks.description: Peter Voulkos was a Greek-American artist known for his abstract expressionist ceramic sculptures. His work challenged the boundary between fine arts and craft. A summer teaching at Black Mountain College in 1953 dramatically shifted his artistic approach, and he began experimenting with gestural works in raw clay. Remembered as an iconoclast, Voulkos fundamentally transformed the medium, bringing an unprecedented level of expressive freedom to ceramic sculpture. "Large Stack Pot" is an early example of Voulkos’ “Stack Pot” form, developed by the artist throughout the 1970s. Sculptural rather than functional, the pot is composed of wheel-thrown sections stacked into a totemic structure. Voulkos has stretched the traditional form of a vessel beyond utility, tearing openings through the clay that render it unusable. The craggy, fractured surface of this piece is partly glazed and largely raw clay, with drips of glaze creating varied surface textures. (Ceramic; 26.5" x 12" x 10"; Gift of the Estate of Paul J. Smith and Kohler Foundation, Inc.)
artworks.imageCredit: Fuller Craft Museum, photo by Will Howcroft

artworks.title: Vessel
artworks.description: Dolores Lewis Garcia learned traditional pottery making practices from her mother, Lucy Martin Lewis, an acclaimed Acoma Pueblo potter famed for her mastery of fine-line painting. Growing up during a time when Indigenous students were reprimanded for engaging with their culture and speaking their language, Lewis’ upbringing instilled in her the necessity of maintaining knowledge of her culture and its traditions. Traditional methods of making are central to Garcia’s practice; she is an advocate against the use of artificial pigmentation techniques in pottery as well as the use of commercial castware. In her work, Garcia often uses black-on-white designs typical of ancient Anasazi (Pueblo) pottery and has revitalized ancient pottery traditions of the Mimbre people. Dolores Garcia Lewis’ "Vessel" depicts a man holding a baton framed by vertical geometrically patterned bands that wrap around the piece. This work follows in the tradition of black-on-white pottery created by the ancient Mimbre peoples. (Ceramic; 3.5" x 3.5" x 3.5"; Gift of the Estate of Paul J. Smith and Kohler Foundation, Inc.)
artworks.imageCredit: Fuller Craft Museum, photo by Will Howcroft

artworks.title: Mari from the "Flasks of Fiction" series
artworks.description: Bella Feldman’s sculptures have deeply impacted the world of contemporary sculpture. Feldman taught for decades as a Professor at the California College of the Arts, where she developed a practice rooted in explorations of material and form. Her works negotiate the tension between strength and fragility through the mediums of metal and glass, and they often examine the precarity of the human condition and critiques of war and power. Feldman developed the innovative technique of hand-blowing glass into pre-made metal forms, allowing for visceral, often political explorations of constriction and pressure. Part of Feldman’s 'Flasks of Fiction' series, "Mari" was inspired by lamps she saw in Turkish mosques. A commentary on vulnerability, constraint, and seduction, the anthropomorphic glass form is cinched by steel bindings, making it bulge in ways that are elegant yet uncomfortable. The delicate opaque sheen of the glass contrasts with the metal harness that contains it, which appears to squeeze the fragile material rather than support it. Feldman stated “Although my objects are beautiful, they contain an element of threat and of irony…They are made for anxious times.” (Glass; 43" x 13" x 12"; Gift of Anonymous)
artworks.imageCredit: Fuller Craft Museum, photo by Will Howcroft

artworks.title: What's His Worth
artworks.description: Tanya Crane received her MFA in Metalsmithing and Jewelry from the University of Wisconsin, Madison, and her BFA in Metal from the State University of New York, New Paltz. She is currently an Assistant Professor of 3D Foundations, Jewelry, and Sculpture at Long Beach City College in Long Beach, California. Crane’s art challenges the boundaries of traditional jewelry and metalsmithing, exploring powerful themes of identity, race, history, and material culture. In "What’s His Worth," the artist poses a question she contemplates as she examines her relationship with and understanding of her father. The black, gourd-shaped vessel is part of a series by Crane that reflects on the complicated memory of a man who suffered racially motivated profiling and abuse in his youth, spent much of his life incarcerated, and struggled with ALS at the end of his life. This piece “speaks to his multiple incarcerations, and ultimately his bodily incarceration.” The urinal, a utilitarian object, has been transformed into a vessel meant to measure the worth of the artist’s father, but is also deeply tied to bodily function and necessities. The outside of this form is marked with sgraffito tick marks, evoking the tracking of the passage of time while incarcerated. (Metal; 5" x 10" x 6"; Museum Purchase with Funds Provided by the Windgate Foundation)

artworks.title: Enemies, Rebels and Traitors
artworks.medium: Ash wood, sweet grass, birch bark, and archival paper
artworks.description: Theresa Secord is a master basketweaver of the Penobscot Nation. She apprenticed with Madeline Tomer Shay from 1988 to 1993, learning the Penobscot language as well as traditional ash and sweetgrass basketweaving techniques. In 1993, Secord co-founded the Maine Indian Basketmakers Alliance (MIBA), an organization dedicated to the preservation of Indigenous basketweaving knowledge. The great-granddaughter of Philomene Saulis Nelson, an accomplished basketweaver of the Maliseet Nation, Secord inherited her great-grandmother’s tools, which had been handed down in her family for generations, grounding her practice in the traditional forms used by her ancestors. Secord’s baskets are a testament to her mastery of her craft as well as her dedication to a continued intergenerational tradition of Indigenous knowledge sharing. The first in a series entitled 'Historical Truth', "Enemies, Rebels and Traitors" was woven on a wooden basket form that has been in Secord’s family since the late 1800s, continuing a traditional form of basketry and serving as a contemporary commemoration of the struggles faced by the Penobscot people historically. The top of this basket contains excerpts of a 1755 proclamation by King George II of England which defined the Penobscot tribe as “enemies, rebels and traitors,” placing a bounty on the head of every man and woman of the tribe. The inclusion of birch bark strips the woods near the artist’s house in Maine calls back to the method of communication used by Penobscot people historically: leaving notes on trees. This basket thus transcends and maintains its traditional function, serving instead as a deliberate message, remembering an overlooked history and serving as a testament to the endurance of the Penobscot people in the face of colonial violence and methodical attempts to exterminate their population. In the 1980s, the Penobscot reclaimed ownership of 150,000 acres of land. (Fiber; 12" x 8" x 5"; Museum Purchase with Funds Provided by Windgate Foundation)
artworks.imageCredit: Fuller Craft Museum, photo by Will Howcroft
